extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students in mathematics/dynamical systems studying linear ODEs
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and solution methods for linear systems X' = AX in R^n: classification via eigenvalues, canonical forms (real and complex), matrix exponentials, behavior (stable/unstable subspaces, sinks/saddles), harmonic oscillators, repeated eigenvalues, and variation of parameters for forced systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and unstable subspaces (definition and behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subspace spanned by eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues with negative real parts is the stable subspace; the subspace spanned by eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues with positive real parts is the unstable subspace. For a hyperbolic system (no zero eigenvalues), solutions starting in the stable subspace stay in it for all time and tend to the origin as t → ∞; solutions in the unstable subspace move away from the origin; other solutions tend toward the stable subspace as time goes backward and toward the unstable subspace as time increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If A has eigenvalues λ1,...,λk negative and λk+1,...,λn positive then any solution with ck+1=...=cn=0 stays in the span of V1,...,Vk and tends to 0. Use eigenvector basis (or real/imaginary parts) to identify these invariant subspaces and predict long-term behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic system (no zero eigenvalues)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system is hyperbolic if there are no zero eigenvalues of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hyperbolicity implies decomposition into stable and unstable subspaces and typical saddle/sink/source behavior depending on signs of real parts. Check eigenvalues for zero to determine hyperbolicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-dimensional analogues of sink/source/saddle (classification by eigenvalue signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If all eigenvalues have negative real parts the system is a sink (all solutions tend to origin); if all have positive real parts it's a source; if some negative and some positive it is a higher-dimensional saddle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering real eigenvalues (e.g., λ3 < λ2 < λ1 < 0) gives information about tangential direction of approach to origin. Use canonical form to visualize (e.g., sink in 3D when all eigenvalues negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical form for distinct eigenvalues and general solution (real and complex blocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A has distinct eigenvalues (k1 real, k2 complex pairs so n = k1 + 2k2), there exists T with T^{-1}AT block-diagonal with real λj on 1×1 blocks and 2×2 blocks Bj = [[αj, βj],[-βj, αj]] for complex pairs αj ± iβj. The general solution is TY(t) where Y(t) has entries c_j e^{λ_j t} for real eigenvalues and for each complex pair terms of the form e^{α t}(a cos βt + b sin βt) and the corresponding sine/cosine partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columns of T are eigenvectors or real/imaginary parts of complex eigenvectors. Write system in canonical coordinates to read off exponential/oscillatory behavior directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior for nonreal eigenvalues (spirals and oscillations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex conjugate eigenvalues α ± iβ produce solutions e^{α t}(a cos βt + b sin βt) and their sine/cosine complements; sign of α determines decay or growth of the oscillation (spiral sink/source).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 2×2 rotation-dilation blocks Bj to see spiraling (when α ≠ 0) or pure rotations (α=0). Identify stable/unstable subspaces by sign of α (real part).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonic oscillator structure and torus invariant sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A pair of (uncoupled) harmonic oscillators x''_j + ω_j^2 x_j = 0 written as first-order system has eigenvalues ± iω1, ± iω2. In canonical coordinates each (x_j,y_j) pair is periodic with period 2π/ω_j and r_j = sqrt(x_j^2+y_j^2) is constant, so solutions with fixed r1,r2 lie on a torus in R^4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce polar coordinates (r_j, θ_j) to see r_j' = 0 and θ_j' = -ω_j. Dynamics restricted to torus reduce to linear flow on a 2-torus parameterized by θ1,θ2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodicity condition for multi-frequency oscillations (rational ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: The full multi-oscillator solution is periodic if and only if the ratio of frequencies ω2/ω1 is rational: ω2/ω1 = n/m. Then period τ = 2π m / ω1 = 2π n / ω2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the ratio is rational, solutions close after finite m,n windings; if irrational, the trajectory is not periodic (quasiperiodic) and may be dense on the torus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré map on the torus and irrational rotations (orbit density)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the torus flow, the Poincaré map on θ1=0 is f(x0) = x0 + 2π(ω2/ω1) mod 2π. If ω2/ω1 is irrational, this is an irrational rotation of the circle and the orbit of any initial point x0 is dense in the circle (hence the trajectory is dense on the torus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rotation representation to analyze recurrence and density: orbit points x_n = x0 + n·2π(ω2/ω1) mod 2π fill the circle densely when the rotation angle is an irrational multiple of 2π. Proof uses finite circumference and approximations to show arbitrarily close returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated eigenvalues and Jordan-block solutions (polynomial factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: For matrices with repeated real eigenvalues and nontrivial Jordan blocks, solutions include polynomial factors in t times e^{λ t} (e.g., t e^{λt}, t^2 e^{λt}, ...). Example: a 3×3 Jordan block yields x1(t)=c1 e^{λt} + c2 t e^{λt} + c3 (t^2/2) e^{λt}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although polynomial factors appear, if λ<0 exponent dominates and solutions tend to zero. The number of independent eigenvectors determines Jordan structure and canonical forms; invariant subspaces correspond to generalized eigenvectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix exponential definition and absolute convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: exp(A) := sum_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k! for any n×n matrix A; the series converges absolutely (entrywise) for every A, with bounds using ||A|| and comparison to scalar exponential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bounds |a_{ij}^{(k)}| ≤ n^{k-1} a^k with a = max|a_{ij}| to show ∑ |a_{ij}^{(k)}|/k! ≤ exp(n a). Thus exp(A) is well-defined for all A ∈ L(R^n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic properties of matrix exponential
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties: (1) If B = T^{-1} A T then exp(B) = T^{-1} exp(A) T. (2) If A and B commute (AB = BA) then exp(A + B) = exp(A) exp(B). (3) exp(-A) = (exp(A))^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use series identities and binomial theorem (when commuting) and similarity conjugation to transfer exponentiation across coordinate changes. Note that commuting is necessary for exp(A+B)=exp(A)exp(B) in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalues/eigenvectors relation for exp(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AV = λV (V an eigenvector of A), then V is also an eigenvector of exp(A) with eigenvalue e^{λ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply series termwise: exp(A)V = ∑ A^k/k! V = ∑ λ^k/k! V = e^{λ} V. This ties spectral properties of A to those of exp(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental solution formula for X' = AX via matrix exponential
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution of the initial value problem X' = AX, X(0)=X0 is X(t) = exp(tA) X0, and this solution is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate exp(tA)X0 to verify it satisfies the ODE; uniqueness follows by multiplying another solution by exp(-tA) and showing derivative zero. This is the canonical way of solving constant-coefficient linear systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of parameters for nonhomogeneous linear systems
rubrics_metrics.description: For X' = A X + G(t) with A constant and G continuous, a solution with X(0)=X0 is X(t) = exp(tA) [ X0 + ∫_0^t exp(-sA) G(s) ds ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields general solution: homogeneous solution plus particular integral obtained by variation of constants. Practical evaluation depends on ability to compute the integral; method always works in principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness of periodic steady-state for forced damped oscillator
rubrics_metrics.description: For a forced damped harmonic oscillator X' = A X + G(t) with G periodic of period 2π and A having eigenvalues with negative real parts, there is a unique 2π-periodic solution (steady-state). The initial condition X0 satisfying X(0)=X(2π) is X0 = (exp(2πA) - I)^{-1}(-W) where W = exp(2πA) ∫_0^{2π} exp(-sA) G(s) ds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show exp(2πA)-I is invertible because eigenvalues of exp(2πA) are e^{2πλ_j} with |e^{2πλ_j}|<1 when Re λ_j <0. All other solutions decay toward this steady-state as t→∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced undamped oscillator solution structure and quasiperiodicity/resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: For the undamped forced oscillator with forcing cos(ω t), variation of parameters yields solution terms with denominators (ω^2 - 1) (or ω±1), so the general solution is a sum of a 2π-periodic term, a 2π/ω-periodic term, and homogeneous oscillatory part. The solution is periodic iff ω is a rational number; if ω is irrational the motion is quasiperiodic. Special behavior occurs near resonance ω = ±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute integrals explicitly when ω ≠ ±1 to see the particular solution; be cautious of resonance where denominators vanish, requiring different treatment. Use frequency-ratio rationality to decide periodicity.
